name: Algarah
tagline: The road junction above Kalimpong, with Damsang Fort in the forest
meta_description: Algarah guide: Damsang Fort and the Gaeboo Achyok story, the old Jelep La trade road, forest walks, homestays, shared jeeps and 2026 costs from Kalimpong.
summary: Algarah is a small bazaar town at about 1,780 m, 15 km east of Kalimpong, where the roads to Lava, Pedong and Sikkim meet. It sat on the old wool road to Jelep La and is the base for Damsang Fort. Most people pass through; we suggest a half-day stop or a quiet night.
intro: Algarah sits on a ridge about 15 km east of Kalimpong, at roughly 1,780 m, which makes it a good 500 m higher and noticeably cooler than the town. It is the headquarters of the Lava block and a working bazaar: a short street of shops, jeep stands, a primary health centre and schools. Three roads meet here. One runs back to Kalimpong, one climbs south-east to Lava and Gorubathan, and one goes north-east to Pedong, the Reshi river and Sikkim.

That position is why Algarah exists. Before the motor road, mule caravans carrying Tibetan wool came down from Jelep La through Sikkim and Pedong, and passed through Algarah on their way to the godowns of Kalimpong. Today the same junction carries National Highway 717A, which links Bagrakote in the Dooars with Gangtok, and nearly every car going to Lava, Rishyap, Pedong or the Silk Route passes through.

Most travellers stop only for tea. That is a pity, because Algarah has the region's most important Lepcha site, the ruined Damsang Fort, a short drive and walk from the bazaar, and forested ridges with views over the Teesta valley. It is also a cheaper, less crowded place to sleep than Lava, with homestays on the slopes around. For a slow trip, it makes a calm first night out of Kalimpong. Prices here are village prices, and a night costs noticeably less than in Kalimpong.

story.title: Damsang and the road to Jelep La
paras: Lepcha tradition holds that the Lepcha chief Gaeboo Achyok built Damsang Fort on a ridge near Algarah around 1690, to resist the Bhutanese who were pushing into the hills east of the Teesta. Oral histories tell that stones were carried up from the Reshi river, and that Achyok was finally killed by treachery. Bhutan held the area for the next century and a half, and Damsang was later used against the forces of the East India Company. It fell into ruin after the Duar War of 1864–65.

When Bhutan ceded the Kalimpong tract under the Treaty of Sinchula in 1865, Algarah found a new role. It lay on the trade route from Kalimpong to Jelep La, the pass into Tibet's Chumbi Valley, and caravans of mules loaded with wool, furs and yak tails passed through its bazaar for nearly a century. The trade ended after the 1962 war closed the pass. Every 20 December, Lepchas from Kalimpong, Darjeeling and Sikkim still gather at Damsang to remember Gaeboo Achyok.
story.source: Algarah and Gaeboo Achyok articles on Wikipedia; Treaty of Sinchula (1865); Jelep La; Lepcha oral tradition

did_you_know: Algarah is the headquarters of the Lava community development block of Kalimpong district.
Lepchas from Kalimpong, Darjeeling and Sikkim gather at Damsang Fort near Algarah every 20 December to mark the birthday of Gaeboo Achyok.
Algarah lies on the historical trade route from Kalimpong to Tibet via the Jelep La pass, which closed after the 1962 India–China war.
facts: Damsang Fort, road junction, old trade route

highlights.title: Damsang Fort
highlights.text: The stone ruins of Damsang Gadi lie in forest on a ridge between Algarah and Pedong. Lepcha tradition dates the fort to around 1690 and links it to Gaeboo Achyok. Little survives beyond low walls, but the setting, the story and the views make the short walk worth it.

highlights.title: A junction on the wool road
highlights.text: Algarah was a stop for mule caravans travelling between Kalimpong and Jelep La until 1962. Today the roads to Kalimpong, Lava and Pedong meet in its bazaar, and it is the natural place to break the drive to the villages or the Silk Route.

highlights.title: Cooler, quieter nights
highlights.text: At about 1,780 m, Algarah is cooler than Kalimpong and much quieter at night. A handful of homestays on the slopes around the bazaar offer rooms with meals at lower rates than Lava, and some face the Teesta valley and the Sikkim hills.

highlights.title: Forest drives toward Lava
highlights.text: The road from Algarah climbs about 16 km through mixed forest and small villages to Lava. Early in the morning it is good for birds, and in spring rhododendron and magnolia flower along the higher stretches. Ask your driver to stop where the forest is thick.

highlights.title: Bazaar tea and snacks
highlights.text: Algarah's tea stalls and small eateries serve the jeeps that stop on the way to Lava, Pedong and Rhenock. Milk tea, sel roti, momos and thukpa are cheap and fresh, and the morning bustle of the jeep stand is a good slice of hill life.

how_to_reach.text: Any shared jeep from Kalimpong's motor stand to Lava, Pedong or Rhenock passes through Algarah, about 45 minutes and ₹50–80 a seat, indicative for 2026. Jeeps from Lava and Pedong back to Kalimpong also stop here. Morning departures are the most frequent; afternoon jeeps are fewer.

A reserved car from Kalimpong costs about ₹1,000–1,500 one way, or ₹2,500–3,500 for a half-day loop with Damsang Fort and Pedong, indicative for 2026. From NJP or Bagdogra, allow about 3.5 hours and ₹4,000–5,500 per car via Kalimpong.

Bagdogra (IXB) is the nearest working airport and New Jalpaiguri (NJP) the main railhead, both reached via Siliguri. Pakyong airport in Sikkim is closer as the crow flies, but flights there have been irregular; check current status before you travel.

where_to_stay: Algarah has no large hotels. A few simple lodges near the bazaar serve travellers and officials, and a scattering of family homestays on the slopes around town offer rooms with home-cooked meals at modest rates. Quality varies, so ask for recent photos and confirm hot water before you book. For mountain views and pine forest, Sillery Gaon and Icchey Gaon are a short drive away. For a WBFDC lodge, go on to Lava, and for heritage hotels such as Morgan House or Mayfair, stay in Kalimpong and visit Algarah by day.
costs: Tea, sel roti or momos in the bazaar
budget_tip: Ride a ₹50–80 shared jeep from Kalimpong to Algarah, walk or take a short local taxi to Damsang, and catch a passing jeep on to Pedong or Lava instead of paying for a full reserved car.
tips: Carry a light jacket even in April; Algarah is about 500 m higher than Kalimpong and evenings turn cool.
Ask at a bazaar shop for the turn-off to Damsang Fort, as signage is limited.
Morning jeeps from Algarah to Kalimpong fill fast, so be at the stand by 8 am if you need a seat.
Withdraw cash in Kalimpong; ATMs in Algarah may be out of service.
In the monsoon, check the Algarah–Lava road before setting out, as landslides can block it for hours.

experiences.title: Walk to Damsang Fort, the Lepcha stronghold
experiences.cost: Free; local taxi ₹300–600 if needed, indicative
experiences.summary: A short drive from Algarah and a forest walk to the ruins of Damsang Fort, linked in Lepcha tradition to Gaeboo Achyok, who is said to have built it around 1690 to resist Bhutan. Low walls, tall trees and a story every Lepcha in these hills knows.
body: Damsang Fort, also called Damsang Gadi, stands on a forested ridge between Algarah and Pedong. From the road it is a walk of 15–30 minutes, depending on where your driver stops, on a path that can be muddy after rain. What survives is modest: lines of stone walls, overgrown in places, and a clearing among the trees. Do not expect a castle. Come for the place and the story.

Lepcha tradition holds that Gaeboo Achyok, a Lepcha chief, built the fort around 1690 to fight the Bhutanese, and that he was eventually killed by treachery. Bhutan then ruled the area until 1865. The fort was later used against the British and fell into ruin after the Duar War of 1864–65. Many local stories add hidden tunnels and treasure; treat those as legend.

Every 20 December, Lepchas gather here for rituals, speeches and songs on what they keep as Achyok's birthday. On other days you will likely have the ridge to yourself. Wear shoes with grip, carry water and leave nothing behind. Combine the walk with Pedong's 1706 monastery and Cross Hill, or with a night at Sillery Gaon. Go in the morning, when the forest is cool and birds are active, and allow about two hours from Algarah and back.

faqs.q: How do I reach Damsang Fort from Algarah
faqs.a: Damsang Fort lies a short drive from Algarah on the ridge toward Pedong, followed by a walk of about 15–30 minutes through forest. A local taxi from Algarah costs about ₹300–600 for the round trip with waiting, indicative for 2026. Signage is limited, so ask in the bazaar or let your driver guide you.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee for Damsang Fort
faqs.a: No. Damsang Fort is free to visit and has no ticket counter or facilities. There are no toilets or food stalls except on 20 December, when the Lepcha gathering brings stalls. Carry water and snacks, and take any rubbish back with you.

faqs.q: Is Damsang Fort worth visiting
faqs.a: Yes, if you enjoy history and forest walks. The ruins themselves are only low stone walls, but the site is central to Lepcha history and identity, the forest is quiet and the ridge has good views. Pair it with Pedong and Sillery Gaon for a full half-day, rather than making a special trip just for the ruins.

experiences.title: Algarah to Pedong on the old wool road
experiences.cost: Car ₹2,000–3,000 for the half day, indicative
experiences.summary: Drive the stretch of the old Kalimpong–Jelep La trade route from Algarah to Pedong, with stops at Damsang, Pedong's monastery of about 1706 and Cross Hill. A half-day that explains why these small bazaars exist and how Tibetan wool once reached Calcutta.
body: Until the 1962 war, the busiest trade route between India and Tibet ran from Kalimpong east through Algarah and Pedong, down to the Reshi river, through Rhenock and Rongli in Sikkim and up to Jelep La at about 4,270 m. Mule trains carried Tibetan wool south and returned with cloth, metal goods, tea and sugar. Algarah and Pedong were overnight stops where muleteers rested and traders did business.

Today a motor road follows much the same line. Start in Algarah with tea at the jeep stand, then stop at Damsang Fort, the Lepcha ruin on the ridge. Continue to Pedong, about 6 km on, for Sangchen Dorjee Gompa, dated to around 1706 when Bhutan ruled these hills, and Cross Hill, where a French missionary raised a cross in 1882. Both stops are free, and a short walk at each lets you stretch your legs between drives.

The whole loop takes four to five hours with stops. Ask your driver to go slowly and point out the old bridle path where it is visible below the road. If you have time, add the drop to the Reshi river at the Sikkim border, or end the day at a homestay in Sillery Gaon instead of driving back to Kalimpong. A half-day car for this loop costs about ₹2,000–3,000, indicative for 2026, so it pays to share it with another couple or a small family.

faqs.q: Was Algarah part of the Silk Route
faqs.a: Algarah lay on the Kalimpong–Jelep La trade route to Tibet, which travel companies now sell as part of the Silk Route. Some silk did travel this way, but the main trade was Tibetan wool, with furs and yak tails, going south, and cloth, metal goods and tea going north. The route closed after the 1962 India–China war.

faqs.q: How far is Pedong from Algarah
faqs.a: Pedong is about 6 km from Algarah, roughly 15–20 minutes by car, on the road toward the Reshi river and Sikkim. Shared jeeps between Kalimpong and Pedong pass through Algarah, so you can hop between the two for under ₹50, indicative for 2026.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for the Algarah–Pedong road
faqs.a: No. Algarah and Pedong are in Kalimpong district, West Bengal, and need no permit for Indian or foreign visitors. A permit is needed only if you cross into Sikkim beyond the Reshi river and continue to Zuluk and the Old Silk Route. Check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Early birding on the Algarah–Lava road
experiences.summary: Leave Algarah at first light and drive slowly up the forested road toward Lava, stopping at clearings and streams to look for birds. Mixed forest between about 1,800 m and 2,200 m holds laughingthrushes, sunbirds, minivets and barbets, and spring adds rhododendron flowers.
body: The 16 km road from Algarah to Lava climbs from about 1,780 m to 2,200 m through patches of oak, chestnut and other broadleaf forest, cardamom fields and small villages. It is quiet before 8 am, when the first jeeps come through. That makes it a good stretch for a slow birding drive, stopping wherever the forest is thick and getting out to walk short sections on foot.

Common birds at this height include sunbirds, minivets, laughingthrushes, bulbuls, barbets and drongos, and the spring months of March to May bring breeding calls and more activity. In winter, some higher-altitude species move down. A local birding guide, arranged in Lava or through your homestay, will know which bends are productive this season and can identify calls you would miss. Ask for a guide who carries a field guide or app and does not use recorded calls to lure birds.

Carry binoculars, a warm layer and something hot to drink. Keep well off the road when vehicles pass, as the bends are blind. Finish at Lava for breakfast and the monastery, or continue into Neora Valley if you have the forest permit. This works well as a transfer day from Algarah or Kalimpong to Lava. Leave at about 5.30 am in spring and 6 am in winter, and tell your driver the day before that you want to stop often.

faqs.q: What birds can I see between Algarah and Lava
faqs.a: Expect common mid-hill species such as sunbirds, minivets, laughingthrushes, bulbuls, barbets, drongos and tits, with more variety in spring. What you see depends on season, weather and luck. A local guide improves the list a lot. For rarer forest birds, continue into Neora Valley National Park with a permit from Lava.

faqs.q: When is the best time for birding near Lava
faqs.a: March to May is best, when birds are breeding and calling, followed by October to December, when the air is clear and some altitudinal migrants arrive. Go at dawn, before traffic starts. Avoid the monsoon from June to September, when rain, leeches and landslides make roadside birding difficult.

faqs.q: Can I hire a birding guide in Algarah
faqs.a: Guides are easier to find in Lava, where the forest office and lodges have contacts for local naturalists. Ask your homestay in Algarah to arrange one a day ahead. Expect about ₹1,000–1,500 for a morning, indicative for 2026. Agree on start time, route and fee in advance.

experiences.title: Morning at the Algarah jeep stand and bazaar
experiences.best_time: 7–9 am, all year except heavy monsoon days
experiences.summary: Spend an hour in Algarah's bazaar at the busiest time of day, when shared jeeps load for Kalimpong, Lava, Pedong and Rhenock, farmers bring produce and tea stalls fry sel roti. A small, real look at how a hill junction town works.
body: Algarah is at its liveliest between 7 and 9 am. Shared jeeps line up for Kalimpong, Lava, Pedong, Rhenock and sometimes Siliguri, with drivers calling destinations and loading sacks of vegetables, gas cylinders and school bags onto the roofs. Farmers from the villages around bring greens, squash, ginger and oranges in season. It is a working scene, not a show. Most of the produce goes on to Kalimpong's Wednesday and Saturday haat.

Find a tea stall, order milk tea and a sel roti or two, and watch. The bazaar serves a wide ring of villages, so you hear Nepali, Lepcha and sometimes Tibetan. Ask the stall owner about the road you are taking that day; locals know about landslides and roadworks before any website does. Tea costs ₹10–20 and a plate of sel roti or puri with potato curry about ₹40–80, indicative for 2026, so breakfast here is cheaper than at most hotels.

There is nothing to buy as a souvenir beyond pickles, churpi or seasonal fruit, and nothing to pay for beyond your breakfast. Keep this to an hour before moving on to Damsang, Pedong or Lava. If you are travelling by shared jeep, this is also where you will find your seat, so ask about departure times a day ahead. Fares are fixed by the drivers' union and posted at some stands; pay the driver when you get in.

faqs.q: Where do shared jeeps leave from in Algarah
faqs.a: Shared jeeps stop and load in the main bazaar, near the junction where the roads to Kalimpong, Lava and Pedong meet. There is no formal booking office; ask drivers or shopkeepers which vehicle is going where. Morning departures are the most reliable. Fares to Kalimpong run about ₹50–80 a seat, indicative for 2026.

faqs.q: What should I eat in Algarah
faqs.a: Try milk tea with sel roti or puri and potato curry in the morning, and momos, thukpa or a rice and dal meal at lunch. Food is simple and cheap, about ₹50–200 per person, indicative for 2026. For more choice, eat in Kalimpong or Lava.

faqs.q: Is Algarah worth a stop
faqs.a: Yes, for an hour or two. Tea in the bazaar, the short trip to Damsang Fort and the views over the valley give a good feel for the old trade road. If you have only one day, combine Algarah with Pedong, or treat it as a break on the way from Kalimpong to Lava.

faqs.q: How far is Algarah from Kalimpong
faqs.a: Algarah is about 15 km east of Kalimpong, around 45 minutes by road. Shared jeeps heading to Lava, Pedong or Rhenock pass through and charge about ₹50–80 a seat, indicative for 2026. A reserved car costs about ₹1,000–1,500 one way. It sits at about 1,780 m, roughly 500 m higher than Kalimpong.

faqs.q: What is Algarah famous for
faqs.a: Algarah is known for the ruins of Damsang Fort, linked in Lepcha tradition to Gaeboo Achyok and dated to around 1690, and for its place on the old Kalimpong–Jelep La trade route to Tibet. It is also the junction where the roads to Kalimpong, Lava and Pedong meet, and the headquarters of the Lava block.

faqs.q: Should I stay in Algarah or Lava
faqs.a: Stay in Lava if you plan to visit Neora Valley, as the permit office and the WBFDC lodge are there. Choose Algarah, or nearby Icchey Gaon and Sillery Gaon, if you want quieter homestays, lower rates and easy access to Damsang and Pedong. Many travellers simply pass through Algarah between Kalimpong and Lava.

faqs.q: What is the altitude of Algarah
faqs.a: Algarah stands at about 1,780 m, or roughly 5,840 ft. That is about 500 m higher than Kalimpong town and about 400 m lower than Lava. Expect days of around 10–20 °C in spring and autumn and cold nights in winter, when temperatures can drop close to freezing.

faqs.q: Is Algarah on the way to Lava
faqs.a: Yes. The usual road from Kalimpong to Lava goes through Algarah, about 15 km from Kalimpong, then climbs another 16 km or so to Lava. The total is about 32 km and 1.5 hours. Shared jeeps between Kalimpong and Lava stop in Algarah's bazaar.

faqs.q: When is the Gaeboo Achyok celebration at Damsang
faqs.a: It is held every year on 20 December, which Lepchas keep as the birthday of Gaeboo Achyok. Lepchas from Kalimpong, Darjeeling and Sikkim gather at Damsang Fort near Algarah for rituals, speeches and cultural programmes. Visitors can usually attend respectfully; ask locally for that year's timings.

faqs.q: Are there homestays in Algarah
faqs.a: Yes, a small number of family homestays and simple lodges operate in and around Algarah, mostly with meals included, at about ₹1,200–2,000 per person a night, indicative for 2026. They are basic but friendly. For more choice and bigger views, look at Sillery Gaon, Icchey Gaon or Ramdhura nearby.

faqs.q: Can I go from Algarah to Sikkim
faqs.a: Yes. From Algarah the road runs through Pedong to the Reshi river and into Sikkim at Rhenock, the start of the Silk Route to Zuluk and a back road to Gangtok. Indians need only ID to enter Sikkim, but Zuluk needs a special permit through a registered operator, and foreigners need a Sikkim permit. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Algarah good in winter
faqs.a: Yes, if you pack warm clothes. December to February is cold and mostly dry, with clear mornings and good views over the Sikkim hills. Nights can drop near freezing, and homestays rarely have heaters, so carry thermals. Light snow is uncommon at this height but happens in some winters.
